l: Dr. Thorneycroft Huxtable's Priory School, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE PRIORY SCHOOL
s: Dr. Thorneycroft Huxtable's Priory School is a selective preparatory school near Mackleton attended by Lord Saltire. l: the Duke of Holdernesse, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE PRIORY SCHOOL

He visits the Priory School with James Wilder, agrees that Holmes may investigate, and denies knowing of any ransom demand or harmful content in his letter to his son.

l: Lord Saltire, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE PRIORY SCHOOL
s: Lord Saltire is the ten-year-old only son and heir of the Duke of Holdernesse. l: James Wilder, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE PRIORY SCHOOL

l: Heidegger, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE PRIORY SCHOOL
s: Heidegger is the German master at the Priory School and has worked there for two years. He disappears at the same time as Lord Saltire, leaves partly dressed through a second-floor window, and takes his bicycle; no connection between him and Lord Saltire is known.

l: the police, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE PRIORY SCHOOL

l: Mackleton, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE PRIORY SCHOOL

l: Holdernesse Hall, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE PRIORY SCHOOL

s: The abduction and disappearance of Lord Saltire concerns his unexplained absence from the Priory School on the night of May 13th. No ransom demand has been received, and the police investigation has been delayed by a false lead.

l: the flight of Lord Saltire and Heidegger, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE PRIORY SCHOOL

l: the German master's body, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When the nobleman and his secretary had left, my friend flung

l: Heidegger's death, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When the nobleman and his secretary had left, my friend flung

l: the boy's flight, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When the nobleman and his secretary had left, my friend flung

l: the boy's disappearance, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When the nobleman and his secretary had left, my friend flung

Holmes examines the two horses and the smithy before Reuben Hayes confronts them and orders them away. l: Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we were left alone in the stone-flagged kitchen, it was
s: Sherlock Holmes realizes that the cow-tracks vary as though the animal walked, cantered, and galloped, concluding that they are a deliberate blind. l: Dr. Watson, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we were left alone in the stone-flagged kitchen, it was

l: Reuben Hayes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we were left alone in the stone-flagged kitchen, it was

l: James Wilder, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we were left alone in the stone-flagged kitchen, it was

l: the Fighting Cock Inn, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we were left alone in the stone-flagged kitchen, it was
s: The Fighting Cock has a squalid courtyard, a smithy, and stables. Holmes and Watson observe James Wilder and another visitor using what appears to be a private part of the inn, while a dog-cart departs from its stable-yard.

l: the smithy, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we were left alone in the stone-flagged kitchen, it was

l: Lower Gill Moor, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we were left alone in the stone-flagged kitchen, it was
s: The moor contains cow-tracks along the investigators' route, but Holmes and Watson see no cows there. Holmes later crosses the moor with Watson on the way back to the school.

l: cow-tracks, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we were left alone in the stone-flagged kitchen, it was
s: The cow-tracks appear at the morass, along the path, and near where Heidegger met his death. Holmes concludes that their varying patterns imitate walking, cantering, and galloping and were made as a deliberate blind.

l: cows, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we were left alone in the stone-flagged kitchen, it was
s: No cows are seen anywhere on the moor, despite cow-tracks appearing along the route taken by Holmes and Watson.

s: The two rough-haired, unkempt horses are kept in the tumble-down stable of the Fighting Cock. Holmes finds that one has old shoes with new nails, supporting his suspicion that the tracks were artificially produced.

l: the patched-Dunlop bicycle, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we were left alone in the stone-flagged kitchen, it was
s: James Wilder's bicycle is left leaning against the wall of the Fighting Cock. Holmes examines it by matchlight and notices that its Dunlop tire is patched.

l: Heidegger's death, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we were left alone in the stone-flagged kitchen, it was
s: Heidegger's death is identified as one of the places near which cow-tracks were seen.

l: the mystery, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we were left alone in the stone-flagged kitchen, it was
s: Holmes believes that his observations at the Fighting Cock have brought him close to solving the mystery. After sending telegrams, he tells Watson that they will reach the solution before the following evening.

The Duke reveals that James Wilder arranged the kidnapping with Reuben Hayes, while Hayes caused Heidegger’s death and held Lord Saltire at the Fighting Cock Inn. Holmes announces Hayes’s arrest, secures Lord Saltire’s immediate return, and agrees to limit the scandal if the Duke ends his concealment and removes James Wilder from the household. The Duke also promises to reconcile with the Duchess, while James Wilder is to leave for Australia.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, At eleven o’clock next morning my friend and I were walking up
s: Sherlock Holmes confronts the Duke of Holdernesse, identifies him as responsible for concealing Lord Saltire’s whereabouts, and demands the promised reward. He reveals that Reuben Hayes has been arrested, secures orders for Lord Saltire’s return, and agrees not to disclose everything he knows if justice is otherwise served.

l: Dr. Watson, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, At eleven o’clock next morning my friend and I were walking up
s: Dr. John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes to Holdernesse Hall and observes the Duke, James Wilder, and the confrontation. The Duke confirms that Watson and Holmes are the only people initially told about the incident.

l: the Duke of Holdernesse, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, At eleven o’clock next morning my friend and I were walking up
s: The Duke admits that James Wilder is his illegitimate son and that he concealed Wilder’s role in Lord Saltire’s kidnapping and Heidegger’s murder. He acknowledges aiding the escape of Reuben Hayes, agrees to retrieve Lord Saltire, sends James Wilder to Australia, and writes to the Duchess to resume their relationship.

l: James Wilder, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, At eleven o’clock next morning my friend and I were walking up
s: James Wilder arranged Lord Saltire’s abduction with Reuben Hayes because of his hatred of the boy and his desire to inherit the Duke’s estate. l: Lord Saltire, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, At eleven o’clock next morning my friend and I were walking up
s: Lord Saltire was lured to the Ragged Shaw by a note using the Duchess’s name and was taken by Reuben Hayes to the Fighting Cock Inn. He is found safe but horrified by Heidegger’s death, and the Duke orders a carriage to bring him home.

l: Reuben Hayes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, At eleven o’clock next morning my friend and I were walking up
s: Reuben Hayes carried out James Wilder’s kidnapping plan, held Lord Saltire in an upper room at the Fighting Cock Inn, and struck Heidegger with a stick during the pursuit, causing his death. He is arrested at Chesterfield on Holmes’s information and faces the gallows.

l: Heidegger, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, At eleven o’clock next morning my friend and I were walking up
s: Heidegger pursued Reuben Hayes and Lord Saltire after the kidnapping and died when Hayes struck him with a stick. His death exposed the seriousness of the kidnapping scheme and caused James Wilder to confess to the Duke.

l: Holdernesse Hall, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, At eleven o’clock next morning my friend and I were walking up
s: Holdernesse Hall is where Holmes and Watson meet the Duke and discuss Lord Saltire’s kidnapping and Heidegger’s death. The Duke also shows them a museum containing medieval horseshoes designed to counterfeit tracks.

l: the Fighting Cock Inn, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, At eleven o’clock next morning my friend and I were walking up
s: The Fighting Cock Inn, about two miles from Holdernesse Hall’s park gate, is where Reuben Hayes confined Lord Saltire under Mrs. Hayes’s care. The Duke orders a carriage to go there and bring Lord Saltire home.

l: the reward for recovering Lord Saltire, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, At eleven o’clock next morning my friend and I were walking up
s: The reward consists of five thousand pounds for information leading to Lord Saltire’s location and another thousand pounds for naming those holding him. Holmes claims to have earned the six thousand pounds and asks the Duke for a crossed check.

l: Lord Saltire’s kidnapping, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, At eleven o’clock next morning my friend and I were walking up
s: Lord Saltire’s kidnapping was planned by James Wilder and carried out with Reuben Hayes’s assistance. Wilder deceived him with a false message involving the Duchess, and Hayes transported him to the Fighting Cock Inn to be held there.

l: Heidegger's death, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, At eleven o’clock next morning my friend and I were walking up
s: Heidegger died after Reuben Hayes struck him with a stick while Hayes and Lord Saltire were being pursued. News of the death prompted James Wilder’s confession and led Holmes to pursue Hayes.

l: Heidegger’s murder, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, At eleven o’clock next morning my friend and I were walking up
s: Heidegger’s murder was committed by Reuben Hayes during the escape after Lord Saltire’s kidnapping. The Duke argues that James Wilder did not know of or directly participate in the killing, but Holmes holds Wilder morally responsible because the murder arose from his crime.

l: James Wilder’s confession, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, At eleven o’clock next morning my friend and I were walking up
s: James Wilder voluntarily confessed to the Duke after learning that Heidegger had died. He admitted arranging Lord Saltire’s kidnapping and then asked the Duke to keep the matter secret for three days so Hayes could escape.

l: Reuben Hayes’s arrest, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, At eleven o’clock next morning my friend and I were walking up
s: Reuben Hayes was arrested at Chesterfield at eleven o’clock the previous night on Holmes’s information. Holmes receives confirmation from the local police before leaving the school.

l: the Duke’s concealment of the crime, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, At eleven o’clock next morning my friend and I were walking up
s: The Duke concealed James Wilder’s involvement, delayed reporting Lord Saltire’s location, and aided Hayes’s escape to protect Wilder. Holmes tells him that this amounted to condoning a felony and aiding a murderer, and requires him to retrieve Lord Saltire before offering further discretion.

l: The Return of Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF BLACK PETER
s: Sherlock Holmes prepares to investigate the death of Captain Peter Carey at Woodman's Lee after Stanley Hopkins reports that the case has made no progress. Carey, a violent former sealer known as Black Peter, was found dead in his cabin with a harpoon driven through his chest. Evidence includes a tobacco pouch, a notebook containing initials and lists of securities, a sheath-knife, and a bottle of rum with two dirty glasses. Holmes agrees to travel to Forest Row with Dr. Watson and Hopkins to examine the scene.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF BLACK PETER
s: Sherlock Holmes has been investigating the tragedy at Woodman's Lee under disguises and names, and he tests his ability to kill a pig with a barbed-headed spear. After hearing Stanley Hopkins's account and examining the evidence, he agrees to visit Peter Carey's cabin with Hopkins and Dr. Watson.

l: Dr. Watson, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF BLACK PETER
s: Dr. Watson narrates the account and hears Stanley Hopkins describe the death of Captain Peter Carey. He is invited by Sherlock Holmes to accompany him and Hopkins to Forest Row.

l: Stanley Hopkins, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF BLACK PETER
s: Stanley Hopkins reports absolute failure in the investigation into Peter Carey's death and asks Sherlock Holmes for help. He describes the crime scene and its evidence, including the harpoon, tobacco pouch, notebook, sheath-knife, rum bottle, and glasses.

l: Captain Peter Carey, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF BLACK PETER
s: Captain Peter Carey was a successful seal and whale fisher who commanded the steam sealer Sea Unicorn before retiring in 1884. Known as Black Peter, he was a violent, intermittent drunkard who abused his family and neighbours. He was found dead in his cabin with a harpoon driven through his chest.

l: Woodman's Lee tragedy, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF BLACK PETER
s: The Woodman's Lee tragedy concerns the unexplained death of Captain Peter Carey at his Sussex residence. Sherlock Holmes has been investigating it before Stanley Hopkins asks him to take a direct look at the case.

l: Captain Peter Carey's murder, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF BLACK PETER
s: Captain Peter Carey was murdered in his cabin at about two o'clock in the morning. He was fully dressed, apparently expecting someone, and was killed with a harpoon taken from a rack; no footprints were found inside or outside.

l: the inquest into Peter Carey's death, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF BLACK PETER
s: The inquest established details including the harpoon taken from the wall, the bottle of rum and two dirty glasses, the tobacco pouch, and the sheath-knife. The notebook found at the scene did not appear at the inquest.

l: Peter Carey's cabin, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF BLACK PETER
s: Peter Carey's cabin was a locked, single-roomed wooden hut where he slept alone and allowed no one else to enter. It contained a bunk, sea-chest, maps, charts, logbooks, a picture of the Sea Unicorn, and the harpoon-pinned body of Carey.

l: Woodman's Lee, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF BLACK PETER
s: Woodman's Lee was Captain Peter Carey's residence near Forest Row, Sussex, where he lived for six years before his death. The cabin in which he was murdered stood a few hundred yards from the house.

l: Forest Row, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF BLACK PETER
s: Forest Row was the nearby village from which the stonemason Slater walked past Woodman's Lee. Stanley Hopkins proposes that Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson travel there to inspect the crime scene.

l: the Sea Unicorn, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF BLACK PETER
s: The Sea Unicorn was a steam sealer from Dundee commanded by Captain Peter Carey in 1883. A picture of the vessel was kept in Carey's cabin, and the harpoon used in the murder was engraved with its name.

l: harpoon, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF BLACK PETER
s: A harpoon was taken from a rack in Peter Carey's cabin and driven through his chest into the wall behind him. Two other harpoons remained on the rack, which had a vacant place for the weapon used in the murder.

l: sealskin tobacco-pouch, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF BLACK PETER
s: A coarse sealskin tobacco pouch marked with Peter Carey's initials was found in the middle of the table. It contained half an ounce of strong ship's tobacco, although no pipe was found.

l: Peter Carey's notebook, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF BLACK PETER
s: Peter Carey's notebook had the initials J.H.N. and the date 1883 on its first page, followed by C.P.R. and lists of securities associated with Argentina, Costa Rica, and San Paulo. It was found on the floor near the door with a bloodstain on the side facing the boards, suggesting that it was dropped after the crime.

l: Peter Carey's sheath-knife, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF BLACK PETER
s: Peter Carey's sheath-knife was found still in its sheath at the feet of his body. His wife identified it as his property.

l: rum bottle, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF BLACK PETER
s: A bottle of rum and two dirty glasses stood on the table in Peter Carey's cabin, suggesting that Carey had been meeting or expecting someone. A tantalus containing brandy and whisky was also present, but its decanters were full.

l: the investigation, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF BLACK PETER
s: The investigation had made no progress under Stanley Hopkins. Holmes questions the evidence, considers the notebook potentially important because of its references to valuable securities, and agrees to examine the scene in person.

l: The Return of Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Alighting at the small wayside station, we drove for some miles
s: Sherlock Holmes, John Watson, and Stanley Hopkins stake out Captain Peter Carey's hut after discovering that someone tried to force entry. They capture John Hopley Neligan, who says he came to inspect the logbooks for evidence concerning his father's disappearance and the reappearance of his father's securities. Neligan is taken toward the police station while Holmes and Watson are thanked for their assistance.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Alighting at the small wayside station, we drove for some miles
s: Sherlock Holmes examines the attempted forced entry, infers that the visitor will return with a stronger tool, and helps arrange the stakeout. l: Dr. Watson, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Alighting at the small wayside station, we drove for some miles
s: John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes and Stanley Hopkins to Sussex and helps conceal himself outside Captain Peter Carey's hut. He observes the nocturnal visitor, his capture, and Neligan's account of his family's connection to the securities.

l: Stanley Hopkins, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Alighting at the small wayside station, we drove for some miles
s: Stanley Hopkins leads Holmes and Watson to the scene, identifies the signs of forced entry, and joins the stakeout. He captures John Hopley Neligan, questions him, produces Neligan's bloodstained notebook, and takes him toward the police station.

l: Captain Peter Carey, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Alighting at the small wayside station, we drove for some miles
s: Captain Peter Carey was the murdered owner of the hut. He had commanded the whaler Sea Unicorn and was identified as the original seller of some securities connected with Neligan's father.

l: John Hopley Neligan, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Alighting at the small wayside station, we drove for some miles
s: John Hopley Neligan secretly enters Captain Peter Carey's hut to search the logbooks for information about his father's fate. He claims innocence in Carey's death, but Hopkins finds his initialed notebook with a bloodstain on its cover, and Neligan is taken into custody.

l: Neligan's father, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Alighting at the small wayside station, we drove for some miles
s: Neligan's father was involved in the failure of Dawson and Neligan, which was publicly attributed to his theft and disappearance. He left by yacht for Norway carrying securities, vanished, and was later suspected by his son of having encountered Captain Peter Carey's ship.

l: Sussex, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Alighting at the small wayside station, we drove for some miles
s: Sussex is where Captain Peter Carey's house and hut are located, amid the remains of the old weald and former iron-working country. John Hopley Neligan came there to investigate Carey.

l: Captain Peter Carey's hut, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Alighting at the small wayside station, we drove for some miles
s: Captain Peter Carey's hut is a small wooden dwelling near the road, surrounded on three sides by bushes, and the scene of his murder. Someone tries to force its door and window, and John Hopley Neligan is later caught inside searching it.

l: the Sea Unicorn, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Alighting at the small wayside station, we drove for some miles
s: The Sea Unicorn was the vessel commanded by Captain Peter Carey. John Hopley Neligan hopes its logbooks will reveal what happened in August 1883, when his father disappeared.

l: Peter Carey's logbooks, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Alighting at the small wayside station, we drove for some miles
s: The logbooks of the Sea Unicorn are kept in Captain Peter Carey's hut. Neligan searches one for the August 1883 entry, but says that the pages dealing with that month have been torn out.

l: Neligan's notebook, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Alighting at the small wayside station, we drove for some miles
s: Neligan's notebook is found by Stanley Hopkins with John Hopley Neligan's initials on the first leaf and a bloodstain on its cover. Neligan says he thought he had lost it at the hotel.

l: Canadian Pacific Railway securities, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Alighting at the small wayside station, we drove for some miles
s: Neligan's father left with securities, intending to realize them and repay his creditors. Some later reappeared on the London market, and the original seller was traced to Captain Peter Carey.

l: Peter Carey's killing, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Alighting at the small wayside station, we drove for some miles
s: The murder of Captain Peter Carey occurred in his hut, where he was pinned against the wall with one of his own harpoons. The unit does not establish who killed him, though John Hopley Neligan is arrested after a bloodstained notebook bearing his initials is found.

l: the attempted burglary, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Alighting at the small wayside station, we drove for some miles
s: The attempted burglary involves someone cutting the woodwork of the hut's door and trying to force its window. Holmes predicts that the intruder will return with a better tool, and the returning visitor proves to be John Hopley Neligan.

l: the disappearance of Neligan's father, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Alighting at the small wayside station, we drove for some miles
s: Neligan's father disappears after sailing toward Norway in his yacht with securities aboard. Neligan believes the yacht may have been blown north and encountered Captain Peter Carey's ship, but the fate of his father remains unresolved because the relevant logbook pages are missing.

l: the sale of the securities, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Alighting at the small wayside station, we drove for some miles
s: The securities carried away by Neligan's father later appear on the London market. Investigation identifies Captain Peter Carey as their original seller, which leads Neligan to seek evidence that his father did not sell them for personal profit.

l: the investigation, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Alighting at the small wayside station, we drove for some miles
s: The investigation examines Captain Peter Carey's murder, the forced entry into his hut, the missing logbook pages, and the history of the securities. Holmes, Watson, and Hopkins stake out the hut and capture Neligan, while Hopkins treats the bloodstained notebook as significant evidence against him.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, “Well, Watson, what do you think of it?” asked Holmes, as we
s: Sherlock Holmes rejects Hopkins’s explanation of Peter Carey’s killing because young Neligan could not have delivered the immensely powerful harpoon blow. Holmes handcuffs Cairns and explains that the evidence points to him as the true killer, while advising Hopkins to release young Neligan.

l: Dr. Watson, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, “Well, Watson, what do you think of it?” asked Holmes, as we
s: Dr. Watson travels with Holmes, attends the breakfast with Hopkins, and helps Holmes restrain Patrick Cairns. Holmes refers to Watson’s knowledge of his having practiced driving a harpoon through a body.

l: Stanley Hopkins, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, “Well, Watson, what do you think of it?” asked Holmes, as we
s: Inspector Stanley Hopkins believes that young Neligan’s notebook provides sufficient evidence that Neligan killed Peter Carey. Holmes disproves this theory, captures Patrick Cairns, and tells Hopkins to obtain Neligan’s release; Hopkins acknowledges Holmes’s superior reasoning.

l: Patrick Cairns, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, “Well, Watson, what do you think of it?” asked Holmes, as we
s: Patrick Cairns is a powerful Dundee seaman and harpooner who served twenty-six voyages, including service aboard the Sea Unicorn. Holmes identifies him as the man who killed Peter Carey, lures him to Baker Street, and arrests him after a physical struggle. Cairns states that he harpooned Carey in self-defense when Carey attacked him with a knife.

l: Captain Peter Carey, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, “Well, Watson, what do you think of it?” asked Holmes, as we
s: Peter Carey, known as Black Peter, was master of the Sea Unicorn and later lived at a hut near Woodman’s Lee. Cairns says Carey murdered a landsman at sea for the contents of a tin box and later attacked Cairns with a knife before Cairns killed him with a harpoon.

l: John Hopley Neligan, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, “Well, Watson, what do you think of it?” asked Holmes, as we
s: Young Neligan was present near the time of Peter Carey’s death and had a notebook concerning securities that Carey may have possessed. Hopkins wrongly concludes that Neligan killed Carey, but Holmes determines that Neligan merely entered the hut after the killing and tells Hopkins to secure his release.

l: harpoon, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, “Well, Watson, what do you think of it?” asked Holmes, as we
s: The harpoon was the weapon used to kill Peter Carey, and its head was driven deeply into the wall with great force. Holmes demonstrates that such a blow required a strong, practiced arm, using this fact to rule out young Neligan and identify a seasoned harpooner.

l: Peter Carey's notebook, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, “Well, Watson, what do you think of it?” asked Holmes, as we
s: The notebook found in connection with the case belonged to young Neligan and listed securities, some marked with ticks. Hopkins treats it as evidence that Neligan went to Peter Carey’s hut to recover securities, but Holmes says it could mislead the investigation.

l: tin box, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, “Well, Watson, what do you think of it?” asked Holmes, as we
s: The tin box belonged to a landsman whom Peter Carey took aboard the Sea Unicorn and later threw overboard. Cairns found the box in Carey’s hut after killing him and took it, but discovered that it contained only papers rather than money; Holmes says it should be returned to young Neligan.

l: criminal investigation, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, “Well, Watson, what do you think of it?” asked Holmes, as we
s: Holmes identifies considering and preparing for an alternative as the first rule of criminal investigation. He criticizes Hopkins for focusing exclusively on young Neligan and instead follows clues pointing to a seaman connected with Peter Carey’s former ship.

l: Peter Carey's killing, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, “Well, Watson, what do you think of it?” asked Holmes, as we
s: Peter Carey’s killing was initially attributed by Inspector Stanley Hopkins to young Neligan, but Holmes shows that this is intrinsically impossible because of the strength required to use the harpoon. Patrick Cairns admits killing Carey after Carey attacked him, describing the act as self-defense rather than murder.

l: The Return of Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF CHARLES AUGUSTUS MILVERTON
s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson meet Charles Augustus Milverton, whom Holmes identifies as London’s most dangerous blackmailer. Milverton demands seven thousand pounds to withhold compromising letters written by Lady Eva Blackwell, whose marriage to the Earl of Dovercourt is threatened. After negotiations fail, Holmes disguises himself as a workman, gathers information from Milverton’s housemaid, and decides to recover the letters by burglary. Watson insists on joining Holmes in the planned raid on Appledore Towers.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF CHARLES AUGUSTUS MILVERTON
s: Sherlock Holmes negotiates with Charles Augustus Milverton on Lady Eva Blackwell’s behalf but cannot reduce the demand for the compromising letters. He disguises himself as a workman named Escott to gather information about Milverton’s house, then plans to burgle it with Dr. Watson.

l: Dr. Watson, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF CHARLES AUGUSTUS MILVERTON
s: Dr. Watson hears Holmes explain Milverton’s methods and observes the failed negotiation. Although he disapproves of the planned burglary, he insists on accompanying Holmes and prepares rubber-soled shoes and black silk masks.

l: Charles Augustus Milverton, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF CHARLES AUGUSTUS MILVERTON
s: Charles Augustus Milverton is described as a wealthy, cunning blackmailer who buys compromising letters and uses them to extort money from people of wealth and position. He demands seven thousand pounds from Lady Eva Blackwell and threatens to expose her letters if the money is not paid.

l: Lady Eva Blackwell, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF CHARLES AUGUSTUS MILVERTON
s: Lady Eva Blackwell is the client whose case Holmes handles. She is engaged to the Earl of Dovercourt, but Milverton possesses imprudent letters she wrote to an impecunious young squire and threatens to use them to break off the marriage.

l: Appledore Towers, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF CHARLES AUGUSTUS MILVERTON
s: Appledore Towers is Charles Augustus Milverton’s house in Hampstead. Holmes learns its layout and plans to enter it at night to recover Lady Eva’s letters.

l: blackmail, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF CHARLES AUGUSTUS MILVERTON
s: Blackmail is presented as Charles Augustus Milverton’s method of buying compromising letters and threatening exposure to extract large sums of money. Holmes considers taking back materials used for this illegal purpose morally justifiable, though technically criminal.

l: Lady Eva’s threatened marriage, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF CHARLES AUGUSTUS MILVERTON
s: Lady Eva’s marriage to the Earl of Dovercourt is scheduled for the 18th, but Milverton threatens to prevent it by sending her imprudent letters to the Earl unless seven thousand pounds is paid by the 14th.

l: Holmes’s campaign against Milverton, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF CHARLES AUGUSTUS MILVERTON
s: Holmes begins a campaign against Milverton after the negotiation fails. He disguises himself as a rising plumber named Escott, courts Milverton’s housemaid to obtain information, and then resolves to recover the letters by burglary.

l: planned burglary of Milverton’s house, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF CHARLES AUGUSTUS MILVERTON
s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson plan to burgle Milverton’s house at night and take only the letters used for the blackmail. They intend to leave from Baker Street at eleven, reach Appledore Towers before midnight, and return with the letters if the operation succeeds.

l: compromising letters, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF CHARLES AUGUSTUS MILVERTON
s: The compromising letters were written by Lady Eva Blackwell to an impecunious young squire. Milverton says they are imprudent and would be sufficient to cause the Earl of Dovercourt to break off the marriage.

l: Milverton’s blackmail demands, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF CHARLES AUGUSTUS MILVERTON
s: Milverton demands seven thousand pounds for the return or suppression of Lady Eva Blackwell’s letters. He refuses Holmes’s offer of two thousand pounds and states that he will send the letters to the Earl if the money is not paid by the 14th.

l: The Return of Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I put on our dress-clothes, so that we might appear to
s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. John Watson break into Charles Milverton’s house in Hampstead to destroy blackmail documents held in his safe. While they hide in Milverton’s study, an unnamed woman arrives and shoots Milverton in revenge for the death of her husband, whom Milverton had driven to suicide. Holmes and Watson burn the documents and escape, while Lestrade later investigates the murder and suspects two masked men. Holmes refuses to assist the police and recognizes the avenging woman as the widow of a great nobleman and statesman, whose title is not named.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I put on our dress-clothes, so that we might appear to
s: Sherlock Holmes disguises himself with Dr. John Watson and breaks into Charles Milverton’s house to open the safe and destroy the blackmail documents. He hides from Milverton and restrains Watson from intervening when the unnamed woman shoots Milverton. Afterward, Holmes burns the documents, escapes with Watson, refuses Lestrade’s request to investigate, and recognizes the avenging woman from a photograph.

l: Dr. Watson, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I put on our dress-clothes, so that we might appear to
s: Dr. John Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes during the burglary, stands guard in Milverton’s study, and hides behind the window curtains when Milverton enters. He witnesses the woman’s revenge, helps Holmes burn the documents and escape, and later hears Lestrade describe the suspected second masked criminal.

l: Charles Augustus Milverton, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I put on our dress-clothes, so that we might appear to
s: Charles Milverton is a blackmailer who keeps compromising papers in a safe in his study. An unnamed woman whose husband died after Milverton sent him her letters shoots him repeatedly in the study, and he dies there.

l: the unnamed avenging woman, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I put on our dress-clothes, so that we might appear to
s: The unnamed avenging woman visits Charles Milverton at night, reveals that he ruined her life and caused her husband’s death, and shoots him with a revolver. She leaves immediately after confirming that he is dead.

l: Countess d’Albert, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I put on our dress-clothes, so that we might appear to
s: Countess d’Albert is the subject of five letters that allegedly compromise her. The unnamed woman says she wants to sell the letters to Charles Milverton, who is prepared to buy them.

l: Hampstead, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I put on our dress-clothes, so that we might appear to
s: Hampstead is where Charles Milverton’s house is located and where the shooting, burglary, and escape occur. Lestrade later comes to Holmes’s rooms to discuss the Hampstead murder.

l: Milverton’s house, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I put on our dress-clothes, so that we might appear to
s: Milverton’s house is a large property in Hampstead with a garden, veranda, conservatory, and several rooms. Holmes and Watson enter through the greenhouse, hide in the study, and escape over a garden wall while the household pursues them.

l: Milverton’s study, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I put on our dress-clothes, so that we might appear to
s: Milverton’s study contains the safe, a desk, a fireplace, and a door leading to his bedroom and the veranda. Holmes and Watson break into it, hide behind its curtains, and witness Milverton’s murder there.

l: the safe, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I put on our dress-clothes, so that we might appear to
s: The safe in Milverton’s study contains packets of papers tied, sealed, and inscribed. Holmes opens it with specialized tools, and after the shooting he empties it by throwing all the papers into the fire.

l: the blackmail documents, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I put on our dress-clothes, so that we might appear to
s: The blackmail documents are stored in Milverton’s safe and contain reputationally damaging material about several women. Holmes burns all of them after Milverton’s death, preventing their further use.

l: the five letters compromising Countess d’Albert, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I put on our dress-clothes, so that we might appear to
s: The five letters are offered for sale to Charles Milverton by the unnamed woman. Their contents are never examined because the woman shoots Milverton before the transaction is completed, and Holmes later burns the blackmail papers.

l: the revolver, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I put on our dress-clothes, so that we might appear to
s: The unnamed avenging woman draws a small revolver from her clothing and fires repeatedly at Charles Milverton at close range. She leaves with it after Milverton falls dead.

l: the murder of Charles Milverton, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I put on our dress-clothes, so that we might appear to
s: The murder of Charles Milverton occurs in his study when the unnamed woman shoots him in revenge for the destruction of her life and her husband’s death. Lestrade investigates the case and believes two masked criminals were involved because Holmes and Watson were present and burned the documents.

l: blackmail, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I put on our dress-clothes, so that we might appear to
s: Blackmail is Charles Milverton’s method of holding compromising papers over people and demanding payment. His blackmail has ruined lives, including that of the unnamed woman, and Holmes regards him as a dangerous man.

l: private revenge, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Holmes and I put on our dress-clothes, so that we might appear to
s: Private revenge is presented by Holmes as potentially justified when the law cannot touch certain crimes. He says his sympathies are with the criminals rather than Charles Milverton, whose killing avenges the harm caused by his blackmail.

l: The Return of Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SIX NAPOLEONS
s: Inspector Lestrade tells Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson about a series of burglaries in London in which plaster busts of Napoleon the First are destroyed, including two busts taken from Dr. Barnicot's residences on Kennington Road and Lower Brixton Road. A third bust is later taken from Mr. Horace Harker's house at 131 Pitt Street, where an unidentified man is found murdered outside. Holmes examines the destruction sites, the bust fragments, and a photograph found on the dead man, and begins pursuing his own line of investigation.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SIX NAPOLEONS
s: Sherlock Holmes listens to Inspector Lestrade's account of the Napoleon bust destruction series and identifies a method in the image-breaker's actions. He examines the Pitt Street scene, the bust fragments, and the photograph found on the dead man, while suggesting that the busts have greater significance than their apparent value.

l: Dr. Watson, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SIX NAPOLEONS
s: Dr. Watson hears Lestrade's account and proposes that the destruction may result from an idée fixe or monomania directed against Napoleon the First. He accompanies Holmes to Pitt Street and the garden where Mr. Harker's bust was destroyed.

l: Inspector Lestrade, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SIX NAPOLEONS
s: Inspector Lestrade reports the destruction of three identical Napoleon busts and later summons Holmes to 131 Pitt Street after a murder occurs there. He investigates the unidentified dead man, the destroyed bust, and the circumstances surrounding the apparent burglary.

l: Mr. Horace Harker, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SIX NAPOLEONS
s: Mr. Horace Harker, a journalist living at 131 Pitt Street, owns a plaster bust of Napoleon that was taken from his mantelpiece during the night. He hears a disturbance and a terrible yell, then finds an unidentified murdered man outside his front door and reports the events to Lestrade, Holmes, and Watson.

l: Napoleon the First, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SIX NAPOLEONS
s: Napoleon the First is the subject of the busts that the unknown image-breaker systematically destroys. Lestrade initially suspects that the destruction reflects a hatred or delusion directed against him.

l: London, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SIX NAPOLEONS
s: London is the setting for the bust destruction series, with incidents occurring in several districts, including Kennington Road, Lower Brixton Road, and Pitt Street. Holmes notes that hundreds of statues of Napoleon may exist in London.

l: Kennington Road, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SIX NAPOLEONS
s: Kennington Road contains Morse Hudson's shop, where the first Napoleon bust is destroyed, and Dr. Barnicot's principal residence, which is later burgled. The bust taken from Dr. Barnicot's hall is carried into the garden and smashed against a wall.

l: Pitt Street, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SIX NAPOLEONS
s: Pitt Street is the location of Mr. Horace Harker's house, where the image-breaker removes a Napoleon bust and an unidentified man is found murdered outside. Holmes observes that the bust was carried to a nearby empty house's garden and destroyed under a street lamp.

l: Napoleon bust, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SIX NAPOLEONS
s: A plaster Napoleon bust is destroyed at Morse Hudson's shop, and another bust of the same type is taken from Mr. Horace Harker's house after a nighttime intrusion. Harker's bust is later found broken into fragments in the garden of an empty house in Campden House Road.

l: Napoleon busts (Dr. Barnicot's collection), The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SIX NAPOLEONS
s: Dr. Barnicot purchased two duplicate plaster casts of Devine's famous head of Napoleon, placing one in his Kennington Road hall and the other in his Lower Brixton Road surgery. Both are destroyed during separate nighttime intrusions, and they were made from the same mould as the bust destroyed at Morse Hudson's shop.

l: Pietro Venucci, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SIX NAPOLEONS
s: The dead man found outside 131 Pitt Street is tall, sunburned, powerful, and apparently under thirty, but poorly dressed and unidentified. His throat has been cut, and a horn-handled clasp knife, an apple, string, a shilling map of London, and a photograph are found near or on him.

l: image-breaker, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SIX NAPOLEONS
s: The image-breaker enters or approaches several premises to locate and destroy plaster busts of Napoleon the First. The person removes busts before breaking them when circumstances require, avoids darker locations, and may have been involved in the events at 131 Pitt Street.

l: Napoleon bust destruction series, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SIX NAPOLEONS
s: The series begins with a bust destroyed at Morse Hudson's shop and continues with the two identical busts belonging to Dr. Barnicot. It later reaches Mr. Horace Harker's house, where the bust's removal coincides with the murder of an unidentified man.

l: burglary of Dr. Barnicot's residences, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SIX NAPOLEONS
s: Dr. Barnicot's Kennington Road residence is burgled, but the only item taken is the Napoleon bust from his hall, which is smashed in the garden. His Lower Brixton Road surgery is also entered, and the duplicate bust on the mantelpiece is smashed where it stood.

l: murder at 131 Pitt Street, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SIX NAPOLEONS
s: A murder occurs outside Mr. Horace Harker's house at 131 Pitt Street during an apparent attempt to remove Harker's Napoleon bust. The victim's throat is cut, and the murderer remains unidentified in this unit.

l: photograph of the dead man, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, THE ADVENTURE OF THE SIX NAPOLEONS
s: A snapshot found in the dead man's possession shows an alert, sharp-featured simian man with thick eyebrows and a pronounced lower face resembling a baboon's muzzle. Holmes studies the photograph and keeps it temporarily with Lestrade's permission for further investigation.

l: The Return of Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
s: Sherlock Holmes and Dr. Watson trace the destroyed Napoleon busts from Morse Hudson and Harding Brothers to Gelder & Co., learning that Beppo worked at both establishments and had previously been imprisoned for knifing an Italian. Harding Brothers’ records identify the purchasers of their three busts, including Josiah Brown of Laburnum Villa in Chiswick, and Holmes predicts that Beppo will attack Brown’s bust. Holmes, Watson, and Inspector Lestrade ambush Beppo at Laburnum Villa as he breaks Brown’s bust, and Beppo is arrested with a bloodstained sheath knife. Holmes indicates that the connection between Beppo, the murder of Pietro Venucci, and the destruction of the busts has not yet been fully explained.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
s: Sherlock Holmes investigates the source and destruction of the Napoleon busts, tracing them through Morse Hudson, Harding Brothers, and Gelder & Co. He uses the evening newspaper and a letter to Josiah Brown to lure Beppo into attacking the remaining bust at Laburnum Villa, where he helps arrest him. Holmes examines the broken bust and says that important details of the case remain unresolved.

l: Dr. Watson, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
s: Dr. Watson accompanies Sherlock Holmes on the inquiries at Harding Brothers, Morse Hudson, and Gelder & Co. He helps watch Laburnum Villa, assists in seizing Beppo, and observes Holmes’s investigation of the broken bust.

l: Harding Brothers, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
s: Harding Brothers of Kensington sold three Napoleon busts obtained from Gelder & Co. One was sold to Horace Harker, one to Josiah Brown of Laburnum Lodge, Laburnum Vale, Chiswick, and one to Mr. Sandeford of Lower Grove Road, Reading.

l: Morse Hudson, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
s: Morse Hudson told Holmes and Dr. Watson that he sold two of Dr. Barnicot’s busts and that a third was smashed on his counter. He identified the photograph of Beppo and said Beppo had worked for him as an Italian piece-work man before leaving the previous week.

l: Gelder & Co., The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
s: Gelder & Co. of Stepney supplied Morse Hudson and Harding Brothers with the relevant Napoleon busts. Its manager said the six casts were half of a batch, made in two plaster moulds, and that there was no known reason for them to differ from other casts.

l: Beppo, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
s: Beppo worked for Morse Hudson and had also worked at Gelder & Co., where he was considered a good worker. More than a year earlier he knifed another Italian, received a one-year sentence, and was later sought by Holmes as the person destroying the busts. He is caught breaking Josiah Brown’s bust at Laburnum Villa and is arrested with a long sheath knife bearing recent bloodstains.

l: Kensington, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
s: Kensington is where Harding Brothers operated and where Horace Harker’s bust was destroyed. Holmes and Dr. Watson return there to question Harding Brothers about the busts.

l: Devine’s head of Napoleon, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
s: Devine’s head of Napoleon was the marble original from which hundreds of plaster casts were made at Gelder & Co.

l: Napoleon busts, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
s: The Napoleon busts are plaster casts made from Devine’s head of Napoleon. Several are destroyed in a connected series of incidents, and Holmes expects Beppo to attack the remaining examples.

l: Morse Hudson’s three Napoleon busts, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
s: Morse Hudson received three Napoleon busts from Gelder & Co. two were sold to Dr. Barnicot, while the third was smashed on Hudson’s counter in broad daylight.

l: Harding Brothers’ three Napoleon busts, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
s: Harding Brothers received three Napoleon busts from Gelder & Co. They sold them to Horace Harker, Josiah Brown, and Mr. Sandeford; Brown’s bust is later broken by Beppo at Laburnum Villa.

l: photograph of Beppo, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
s: The photograph is shown to Morse Hudson and the manager of Gelder & Co., who both identify the pictured man as Beppo. Holmes uses it to connect Beppo with the destroyed busts and with the man arrested at Laburnum Villa.

l: Mr. Horace Harker, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
s: Horace Harker bought one of the three Napoleon busts sold by Harding Brothers. His bust was destroyed, and his sensational newspaper account described the incident as a murder by a madman.

l: Josiah Brown, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
s: Josiah Brown bought one of Harding Brothers’ Napoleon busts and lived at Laburnum Villa in Chiswick. After receiving Holmes’s note, he locked the doors of his house and waited for developments while Holmes, Dr. Watson, and Inspector Lestrade watched outside.

l: Laburnum Villa, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
s: Laburnum Villa was Josiah Brown’s house in Chiswick and contained one of Harding Brothers’ remaining Napoleon busts. Beppo entered the house and broke the bust outside, where Holmes, Dr. Watson, and Inspector Lestrade arrested him.

l: evening newspaper, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
s: The evening newspaper reported the Kensington incident under the headline “Kensington Outrage. Murder by a Madman.” It printed a sensational account and repeated the conclusion attributed to Inspector Lestrade and Sherlock Holmes that the events arose from lunacy rather than deliberate crime; Holmes also used it to plant a misleading clue for Beppo.

l: Inspector Lestrade, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
s: Inspector Lestrade identifies the dead man as Pietro Venucci and theorizes that the murder resulted from a Mafia pursuit. He accompanies Holmes and Dr. Watson to Laburnum Villa, helps arrest Beppo, and remains convinced that his Mafia theory will explain the case.

l: Pietro Venucci, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
s: Pietro Venucci is identified as the dead man found in connection with the Kensington incident. Inspector Lestrade says he was from Naples, was a notorious cut-throat connected with the Mafia, and may have been pursuing the man in Beppo’s photograph.

l: Mafia, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
s: The Mafia is described by Inspector Lestrade as a secret political society that enforces its decrees by murder. Lestrade believes Pietro Venucci was pursuing another Italian because that person had broken Mafia rules.

l: murder of Pietro Venucci, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
s: The murder is attributed by Inspector Lestrade to a struggle involving Pietro Venucci and another Italian, whom he believes may be Beppo. Holmes captures Beppo but indicates that the full relationship between the murder and the destroyed busts still requires explanation.

l: destruction of the Napoleon busts, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
s: The destruction affects busts sold through Morse Hudson and Harding Brothers, with Beppo connected to the incidents through his work at the relevant establishments. Holmes arranges surveillance at Laburnum Villa and catches Beppo breaking Josiah Brown’s bust, but his examination finds no visible peculiarity in the plaster fragments.

l: letter from Sherlock Holmes to Josiah Brown, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, Sherlock Holmes and I walked together to the High Street, where
s: Sherlock Holmes sends Josiah Brown an urgent letter by express messenger. Brown follows its instructions by locking every door inside Laburnum Villa and awaiting the expected intruder, enabling Holmes and the others to catch Beppo.

l: The Return of Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we met again next evening, Lestrade was furnished with much
s: Sherlock Holmes buys the last Devine’s Napoleon bust from Mr. Sandeford of Reading and breaks it open, finding the famous black pearl of the Borgias inside. Holmes explains that Beppo concealed the pearl in one of six wet plaster busts while fleeing the police, then later searched for it after his arrest. He connects the pearl’s disappearance with Lucretia Venucci, her brother Pietro, Pietro’s murder, and Beppo’s destruction of the other busts. Inspector Lestrade praises Holmes’s investigation, while Holmes returns immediately to another case.

l: Sherlock Holmes, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we met again next evening, Lestrade was furnished with much
s: Sherlock Holmes purchases the Reading bust from Mr. Sandeford for ten pounds and has the seller transfer every possible right to it. He breaks the bust open and finds the famous black pearl of the Borgias, then explains how he traced it through the six busts and related crimes.

l: Dr. Watson, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we met again next evening, Lestrade was furnished with much
s: Dr. Watson observes Holmes’s uneasiness, excitement, and pleasure at the praise he receives after recovering the pearl. Holmes directs him to place the pearl in the safe and retrieve the papers concerning the Conk-Singleton forgery case.

l: Inspector Lestrade, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we met again next evening, Lestrade was furnished with much
s: Inspector Lestrade supplies Holmes with information about Beppo and witnesses Holmes recover the pearl. He praises the investigation and says that Scotland Yard is proud of Holmes.

l: Beppo, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we met again next evening, Lestrade was furnished with much
s: Beppo is identified as an Italian former sculptor and known criminal who worked at Gelder & Co. He concealed the pearl in a wet Napoleon bust before his arrest, and later tracked the six busts through London, destroying them in search of the hidden jewel.

l: Mr. Sandeford, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we met again next evening, Lestrade was furnished with much
s: Mr. Sandeford, of Reading, owns the last Napoleon bust and brings it to Holmes in an old-fashioned carpet-bag. He sells it for ten pounds after signing away every possible right he had in it.

l: Gelder & Co., The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we met again next evening, Lestrade was furnished with much
s: Gelder & Co. manufactured the six plaster busts of Napoleon at its Stepney establishment. Beppo worked there, and the busts were drying in the passage when he concealed the pearl in one of them.

l: Lucretia Venucci, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we met again next evening, Lestrade was furnished with much
s: Lucretia Venucci was the Italian maid of the Princess and the sister of Pietro. Holmes believes she was connected to the disappearance of the pearl through Pietro and possibly Beppo.

l: Pietro Venucci, The Return of Sherlock Holmes, When we met again next evening, Lestrade was furnished with much
s: Pietro was Lucretia Venucci’s brother and was murdered two nights before this meeting. Holmes believes he was connected with Beppo and the pearl, though he cannot determine whether Beppo stole it from him, acted as his confederate, or served as a go-between.
